title: 08 Probability and combinatorics: Visual Guide
outline: Title: 08 Probability and combinatorics: Visual Guide

1. Dot Product Average | three probability sliders driving a row-times-column product against the values 0, 10 and 100, with a validity badge on the sum and the balance point marked on a number line | an expected value is the familiar dot product of a weight row with a value column, and the sum-to-one rule is what turns that weighted total into an average, so a table whose probabilities miss 1 has no expected value at all

2. Counted Twice | two Venn circles over 30 engineers whose overlap you drag from 0 to 12, with the naive P(A) + P(B) bar sitting above the true union bar and the amber slab between them | the overlapping region is the intersection, and the subtracted term in the addition rule is exactly the copy of it that P(A) and P(B) each counted, going to zero on its own when the events are mutually exclusive

3. Multiply The Stages | a unit-square area model where the width is P(A) and the shaded height is P(B given A), switchable between independent, mutually exclusive and general, with an impossibility check | P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B given A) always, collapsing to the product 0.3 x 0.4 = 0.12 only under independence, while mutually exclusive gives 0 and is the most dependent case there is

4. Order Or Not | n and r sliders showing nPr, nCr and r! with the factorial cancellation written out, and every unordered set drawn expanding into its r! ordered lists | permutations count arrangements and combinations count selections, and the exact factor between them is r!, which is why nCr = nPr / r! is a whole number and why using a permutation for a committee over-counts

5. Long Run Average | a fair die and a skewed 0/10/100 payout spun up to 5,000 times, with the running mean plotted on a log axis against the dashed E[X] line and a tally of observed versus true probabilities | the expected value is the long-run average the running mean converges to, not the most likely value, not the middle value, and not necessarily a value the variable can ever produce
